blocks.text: But in a world where uncertainty around inflation and the prospect of stronger than anticipated economic growth—today, powered by the artificial intelligence build-out—persists, that relationship has turned positive. That means stocks and bonds can rise and fall together.
blocks.section: A calm index, a restless market

blocks.text: As 10-year Treasury yields have risen nearly 80 basis points over the course of the summer, the stock market hasn’t felt the pain at the index level. Whereas the bond market has taken its cue first from hawkish monetary policy, global fiscal debt fears, higher energy prices and now the prospect of rapid economic growth , equities have been more focused on seven straight quarters of corporate earnings growth. The S&P 500 sits ~6% above its 200-day moving average and within about 2% of its record high, yet only ~43% of stocks in the benchmark are trading above their 200-day average. That figure is down from 75% in mid-August. At the same time, 10-year Treasury yields have risen over 60 basis points.
Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of September 30, 2026.
Note: Mag 7 is an equally-weighted basket of Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla.

The chart tracks the price returns since May for three groups: the S&P 500, S&P 500 Utilities and the “Mag 7” basket of large tech stocks. S&P 500 Utilities start out strong, climbing to a peak above 10% in July before steadily falling and ending September around –10%. The S&P 500 stays close to zero throughout, dipping slightly negative in July and August but finishing September with a modest gain of about 2%. The Mag 7 stocks drop sharply early in the summer, hitting lows near –12% in July, but then rebound steadily, ending September up about 7%.

However, today, stocks are moving more independently than normal. This is best displayed in the Cboe 3-month implied correlation index, which measures how closely options traders expect large U.S. stocks to move in sync. The measure currently sits at 11.2, well below the long run average of 41. It offers an opportunity to diversify risk exposure within the equities market itself at both a sector and thematic level.

The correlation started very high in 2020, peaking above 70, then quickly dropped and fluctuated between roughly 30 and 60 through 2021 and 2022. From 2023 onward, the correlation mostly stayed below the dashed line marking the 20-year average at about 40, with occasional brief spikes above that level. In the most recent period, the correlation remains low, hovering in the 10–15 range.
Utilities have long been thought of as a defensive sector of the stock market.
There are few power sources that can handle build-out of that size, which has made utilities providers key enablers of AI .
In response, state governments have put moratoriums on that build-out—something that has weighed on the sector.
Because utilities are often valued for their dividends, higher yields in the Treasury market can compete with this aspect of what the sector has to offer.
S&P 500 Utilities sector

Both lines climb steadily through June and early July, peaking just before the New York data center moratorium is signed. After that point, both the price and P/E ratio begin to decline, with a sharper drop following the Texas data center restrictions announcement in early August.
In a world where bonds provide less diversification than they once did, that dispersion itself may become one of investors’ most valuable tools.
